newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan considering resuming grant aid to China.
newsitem.headline: Japan considering resuming grant aid to China.

text.p: Japan is considering resuming tens of millions of dollars in grant aid to China, suspended last year because of Beijing's nuclear testing, authoritative sources said on Thursday.
The sources stressed if a decision was made to resume the aid it would not in any way be linked to an islands row between China and Japan.
But they did not rule out a positive decision on the aid serving as a useful signal to Beijing of Tokyo's desire not to let the islands row get in the way of overall relations.

The sources said a decision on whether to end the ban now that China has ended its testing programme was awaiting a decision by the coalition government Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto is trying to put together.
"If the political will is there to end the ban, the grant aid could resume before the end of this year," a senior official involved in the decision said.
Japan last year froze the grant aid, worth about seven billion yen ($60 million), as a mainly symbolic protest at China's nuclear test programme.
The bulk of Japanese aid to China, about 580 billion yen ($5.4 billion) in soft loans over the next three years, has never been affected, despite Japanese protests about the testing.
After a nuclear test at the end of July, China announced it was imposing a moratorium on future blasts which was warmly welcomed by Japan, the only country to have suffered a nuclear attack.

The official said some government members were pushing for a quick decision on unfreezing the grant aid -- money for specific projects -- as a timely and symbolic way of defusing tension set off by the islands dispute.

The dispute over the deserted islands in the East China sea claimed by Japan, China and Taiwan has become a major irritant between Tokyo and Beijing and is regarded as one of the most pressing foreign policy issues to be settled by a new Japanese government.
The resource-rich island chain is known by Japan as the Senkakus and called the Diaoyus by Taiwan and China.

On October 7, Taiwan and Hong Kong activists pierced a Japanese maritime cordon and hoisted flags of Taiwan's exiled Republic of China and the arch rival communist People's Republic of China on the islands.
Tokyo voiced regret for what it called the illegal landing and vowed to take necessary measures to stop similar actions.

Last July, Japanese rightists triggered the angry and increasingly nationalistic backlash from ethnic Chinese across Asia by raising Japan's flag and building a lighthouse on the islands to assert Tokyo's claim.
Japan claimed the islands in 1895 and refuses to acknowledge that the dispute is open for discussion with China or Taiwan.
China and Taiwan say the islands have been Chinese territory for centuries and should have been returned after Japan's defeat in World War Two.
There is some concern that political turmoil set off by last Sunday's inconclusive Japanese general election could get in the way of a quick decision on the aid issue.
Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) narrowly missed a majority and is involved in negotiations that could take up to two weeks to form a coalition government.
